Tests: crash-test dummies for your code

A test is a tiny program that checks your program. Test the logic (moving, scoring, saving), not the drawing. Test normal cases and edge cases: the corner, the wall, the empty list, the last life.

Example: tests for a tiny Player

muncher\_demo.py

class Player:
    def __init__(self, row, col):
        self.row = row
        self.col = col
        self.score = 0

    def move(self, grid, d_row, d_col):
        new_row, new_col = self.row + d_row, self.col + d_col
        if grid[new_row][new_col] == "#":
            return False
        self.row, self.col = new_row, new_col
        if grid[new_row][new_col] == "*":
            self.score += 10
            grid[new_row][new_col] = "."
        return True

test\_muncher\_demo.py

from muncher_demo import Player

def make_grid():   # a tiny maze: wall, empty, star, empty, wall
    return [list("#####"), list("#.*.#"), list("#####")]

def test_player_moves_into_an_empty_cell():
    p = Player(1, 1)
    assert p.move(make_grid(), 0, 1) is True
    assert (p.row, p.col) == (1, 2)

def test_walls_block_the_player():          # edge case
    p = Player(1, 1)
    assert p.move(make_grid(), -1, 0) is False
    assert (p.row, p.col) == (1, 1)

def test_eating_a_star_scores_10_once():    # edge case
    grid = make_grid()
    p = Player(1, 1)
    p.move(grid, 0, 1)
    p.move(grid, 0, -1)
    p.move(grid, 0, 1)
    assert p.score == 10

How to run your tests: in Thonny choose Tools → Open system shell..., make sure you are in your project folder, and type python -m pytest -q. Each dot is a passing test; an F is a failing one, with its name and the line that failed.

TipIs my test any good?

Break your code on purpose. Does the test go red? If not, the test is not checking anything. Then fix the code and watch it go green.

Playtest and triage

In a playtest, someone else uses your project while you watch silently and take notes. Every time they get stuck, you learn something. Afterwards, sort the notes into three piles – that is called triage:

For a crash: first write a test that shows the bug, then fix it. The test makes sure it never comes back.

Exercise11.2: Playtest feedback cards

Cut these out (or copy them onto index cards). Fill in one card for each thing you notice while your partner plays.

New words

edge case
An unusual input at the limits: a corner, an empty list, zero, the last life.
playtest
Watching someone use your project to find problems.
triage
Sorting problems by how much they matter, to fix the important ones first.
README
A file that explains what a project is, how to run it and how it works.
usability
How easy something is to use for someone new.
accessibility
Designing so that people with different abilities can use it too.

Homework: Project Studio 2

15–20 minutes. Finish Milestone 4 and get ready for the showcase.

CoreFinish Milestone 4 and prepare your talk

  1. Finish your README.md: title, how to run, controls, how it works (classes, data structure, algorithm, saved file), tests, credits. Commit it.

  2. Fix one more “must fix” or “should fix” bug from your playtest cards. Commit it.

  3. Run all your tests: python -m pytest -q. Number passing: (blank to fill in) (goal: 5 or more)

  4. Fill in the showcase talk card (workbook Exercise 12.1) and practice once out loud with a timer: 2 minutes.

ChallengeAn edge-case hunt

Think like a sneaky player: what could break your project? (Pressing keys very fast, walking into a corner, an empty save file, the last life.) Write a test for one of them. If it fails, fix the code. Commit with a message like Test and fix empty high-score file.

CreativeBox art

Design the box or poster for your project as if it were sold in a shop: the title, one exciting sentence, a picture, and “Made by” with your nickname. Keep it at home – no posting online.

Self-checkSelf-check: tick each box when it is true
